papers.title: A pilot computer-vision model trained to identify slide-mounted scale insect pests from the family Rhizoecidae
papers.abstract: The emerging field of image classification using computer vision has yet to address a rather challenging group of insect pests--soft-bodied insects that are preserved on microscope slides. This includes many notoriously invasive herbivores that have a significant impact on agriculture, such as members of the hemipteran suborder Sternorrhyncha. Using root mealybugs (Hemiptera: Rhizoecidae) as a test case, we gathered high-resolution extended depth of field images from museum specimens and trained a convolutional neural network (CNN) to identify and distinguish among 16 root mealybug species that are encountered as agricultural pests in plant quarantine or greenhouses. A pretrained EfficientNetV2-M model was trained using BioEncoder. Our dataset contained 1,607 images, with 41 to 239 images per category. Performance was improved through the adoption of augmentation techniques. Upon completion of training, the model achieved macro precision, recall, and F1 scores of 80.1%, 79.3%, and 79.1%, respectively. The model demonstrated classification metrics >= 80% for seven species. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) was used to visualize the morphological features associated with the test-image classification. Grad-CAM images highlighted meaningful diagnostic features to distinguish among species rather than focusing on uninformative visual artifacts or specimen damage, demonstrating the models utility for identification purposes. The results suggest that further development of the model should incorporate at least 200 training images per species with a minimum resolution of 600x600 pixels. The model was designed to be adaptable; images can be added to improve its performance, and more species can be incorporated as specimens become available, expanding on the taxonomic breadth of its application. Computer-vision identification tools have the potential to enhance rapid response capabilities in plant quarantine at ports-of-entry in the United States and globally.

papers.title: Shared landscapes, shared risk: Echinococcus multilocularis infection in coyotes is linked to agricultural land and altered green space in a major U.S. metropolitan area
papers.abstract: Alveolar echinococcosis (AE), caused by the tapeworm Echinococcus multilocularis, is among the most lethal zoonotic helminthic diseases affecting humans. Historically rare in North America, human and canine AE cases have risen sharply over the past decade, coinciding with the spread of a more virulent European-type haplotype and the emergence of coyotes (Canis latrans) as a principal definitive host in and around urban centers. Despite growing recognition of E. multilocularis as an emerging public health concern, the host- and landscape-level factors that concentrate infection risk within urban environments remain poorly understood. We used monitoring data from the Chicago metropolitan area to assess E. multilocularis prevalence and test demographic and land cover predictors of infection among urban coyotes. Fecal samples from 85 coyotes were screened via real-time PCR, and land cover association with E. multilocularis infection within individual home ranges or capture-based buffers was investigated using generalized linear models. Overall, 27.1% of coyotes were infected. Infection status was unrelated to age or sex, but coyotes with a greater proportion of agricultural land or altered open land cover, such as golf courses, cemeteries, and manicured parks, within their home ranges had significantly higher odds of infection (ORagriculture = 2.84; ORaltered open spaces = 2.07). These landscapes are also heavily used by people and domestic pets, suggesting elevated potential for zoonotic spillover in human-dominated areas rather than natural or forested habitat. Our findings identify specific, human-accessible landscapes that sustain E. multilocularis transmission in a major U.S. metropolitan area and provide a framework for prioritizing surveillance, targeted anthelmintic intervention, and public health outreach in expanding urban coyote populations across North America.

papers.title: Antenna cells of ascidian larvae are gravity-sensing neurons
papers.abstract: Ascidians are the closest living relatives of vertebrates, and they share a basic body plan including the dorsal central nervous system. The central nervous system of ascidian tadpole larvae controls their swimming behavior. In particular, for the first few hours after hatching, larvae swim upward. Gravity is sensed by an organ called the otolith, which resides in a brain vesicle. Although this sensory information is thought to be transmitted to two antenna cells abutting the otolith, direct evidence that the antenna cells function as gravity-sensory neurons has been lacking. In the present study, we first identified a regulatory element of the Vglut gene that drives expression in antenna cells and otolith-associated ciliated cells. Using this upstream regulatory element, we specifically overexpressed the apoptosis-inducing gene, Bax, in antenna cells and otolith-associated ciliated cells, and succeeded in their targeted ablation. These Bax-overexpressing larvae lost their preference for upward swimming. Because antenna cells have axons and otolith-associated ciliated cells lack neurites, our observation indicates that antenna cells are the sensory neurons for gravity. In addition, our experimental method for targeted disruption of cells using an enhancer element and Bax provides a valuable tool to examine neural circuit functions at cellular resolution.

papers.title: Pufferfish inflation: drivers of axial and hoop skin strain and regional variation across the body
papers.abstract: Pufferfish skin undergoes large multi-axial extensions during defensive inflation behaviour, as water is pumped into the stomach and the fish increases its body volume threefold. This remarkable capacity for deformation thus raises questions on how skin extension is spatially distributed across the body, and how skin extension relates to changes in body volume and stomach pressure. However, directly measuring skin extension remains experimentally challenging, particularly when attempting to preserve the bodys complex 3D geometry and natural multiaxial strain during ex vivo testing. We used biplanar x-ray videography to measure skin strain (fluoromicrometry) and body volume (dynamic digital endocast) simultaneously with stomach pressure recordings during natural and artificial inflations in porcupinefish ( Diodon holocanthus ). We found no significant difference in maximum body volumes (2.66 {+/-} 0.65 times their initial body volume), body dimensions (e.g., dorsoventral height 87.31 {+/-} 0.23 mm), peak pressures (2.45 {+/-} 1.10 kPa), and skin extension at maximum inflation between natural and artificial inflation conditions. In all inflations, volume increased steadily while stomach pressure only increased during the last 25-50% of inflation. Skin extension varied biaxially, with mean strains reaching up to 102% in the axial direction and 146% in the hoop direction as the fish became nearly spherical. The greatest skin extensions occurred most dorsocranially (axial) and ventrolaterally (hoop). Strains in the hoop direction were only significantly different between body regions (defined as dorsal, lateral and ventral), with the greatest hoop strains occurring in the ventral body region. Our findings may provide insight into existing hypotheses regarding the relationship between volume, pressure, and skin structure and behaviour, while also providing direct in vivo measurements to inform biomimetic design.

papers.title: An update on the mosquito fauna of Aguascalientes, Mexico: morphological and molecular identifications, host-feeding patterns, and the removal of Aedes idahoensis (Theobald) from Mexico
papers.abstract: To better understand taxonomic identity and feeding patterns of mosquitoes in all physiographic regions and sub-regions of Aguascalientes, Mexico, we conducted surveillance followed by morphologic analysis and DNA metabarcoding. We targeted the Sierra Madre Occidental, Central Plateau, and Neo-Volcanic Axis. We sampled natural larval habitat for immature stages and adults were collected using Shannon and CDC light traps, mechanical aspirators, and human landing catch method. In addition, curated specimens from Aguascalientes deposited in a local institution were re-examined. Overall, 5,227 mosquito specimens consisting of 357 larvae, 199 larval exuviae, 373 pupal exuviae, 33 pupae, 3,000 females, 1,264 males, and 1 male genitalia were examined using taxonomic keys. Most immature and adult species (n = 20/34 species representing 58.8% coverage) were barcoded for molecular species designation, and a subsample (n = 64) of engorged female mosquitoes were analyzed for blood feeding patterns. Two subfamilies, four tribes, seven genera, 14 subgenera, and 34 species were identified, which one tribe, three genera, nine subgenera, and 22 species are new records. Phylogenetic analysis of specimens from Aguascalientes identified 20 species. Morphological observation of mosquitoes deposited in entomological collections resulted in the removal of Aedesidahoensis from Mexico, leaving the country with a total of 255 species documented. Bloodmeal metabarcoding was successful in 23 mosquitoes of five species, revealing evidence of feeding on more than a single vertebrate species in 17 individuals. Birds were the most common host with the cattle egret (Ardea ibis) found in 18 out of 23 mosquitoes. This update on the taxonomic identity and mosquito richness and feeding patterns from Aguascalientes affords a better understanding of the ecology of medically important mosquito species.

papers.title: What happens when Arctic sea-ice melts? Macroalgae as a summer refuge for sympagic nematode Theristus melnikovi
papers.abstract: Sea ice-associated (sympagic) nematodes are particularly vulnerable to ongoing Arctic sea-ice loss, yet the capacity of these sympagic species to persist in ice-free habitats remains poorly understood. We investigated the summer habitat and taxonomic identity of the sympagic nematode Theristus melnikovi, in Svalbard, using an integrative taxonomic approach. We barcoded 17 morphologically identified nematodes from macroalgae (5), sea-ice (9), and sediment (3). Morphological analysis and phylogenetic reconstruction based on 18S rRNA gene analyses revealed that the macroalgae-associated T. melnikovi represented a habitat-associated phenotypic variation of T. melnikovi rather than a morphotype of the benthic nematode T. acer. Macroalgae-associated specimens were generally shorter and stouter, with proportionally longer tails and shorter anterior structures than their ice-associated counterparts, resulting in a superficial resemblance to T. acer. Despite these morphological differences, molecular analyses consistently placed macroalgae-associated individuals within the T. melnikovi clade and haplotype. Our results highlight that T. melnikovi may have a greater ecological flexibility than previously assumed and macroalgae may offer an alternative (summer) habitat, or refuge, during ice-free periods. This capacity could become increasingly important as Arctic sea-ice duration and extent continue to decline.

papers.title: Repeated coastal observations and molecular confirmation of Alatina grandis (Cubozoa: Alatinidae) in the Gulf of Aqaba, Red Sea
papers.abstract: Cubozoans are rarely documented in the Red Sea, and the taxonomic identity of large alatinid medusae previously reported from the Gulf of Aqaba has remained uncertain. Historical observations from Eilat in 1997 and 2000 were reported as Carybdea alata, although their exceptionally large size was recognized as being within the range of C. grandis (currently Alatina grandis); unresolved carybdeid taxonomy at the time prevented a definitive species-level assignment. Following more than two decades without documented observations, five large alatinid medusae were recorded on separate occasions along the Eilat coastline between July 2025 and August 2026. One specimen was collected, while high-resolution in situ photographs and video recordings of live medusae provided material for morphological assessment. Diagnostic morphological characters were consistent with Alatina grandis, and molecular analysis of the collected specimen independently confirmed its identity as A. grandis. These findings provide the first molecular confirmation of A. grandis from the Gulf of Aqaba and the Red Sea and establish the identity of the alatinid medusae documented during the recent series of observations. The clustering of five observations within one year, following more than two decades without documented occurrences, raises questions regarding the temporal occurrence and distribution of this rarely reported cubozoan in the northern Red Sea.

papers.title: Shifts in the Maternal Gut Microbiome Across Pregnancy are Associated with Energetic Status in Phayre's Leaf Monkeys
papers.abstract: During pregnancy, mothers experience physiological changes that support fetal development, including shifts in energy utilization and increasing insulin resistance during late gestation. While these changes benefit the fetus, they can also impose energetic costs that affect the mother's physical condition and metabolic phenotype. Previous studies suggest that the gut microbiome, a key regulator of female metabolism and energy harvest, may play a critical role in mediating these physiological challenges. In this study, metagenomic sequencing of the gut microbiome of 120 samples revealed dramatic shifts in gut bacterial composition and function associated with pregnancy and lactation in 14 wild Phayre's leaf monkeys, Trachypithecus phayrei crepusculus, from two groups at the Phu Khieo Wildlife Sanctuary, Thailand. Alpha diversity, beta diversity, and taxonomic composition all differed between cycling and the 3rd trimester. Furthermore, bacterial dissimilarity between these states was negatively correlated with postpartum physical condition; that is, mothers whose gut microbiota remained more stable during pregnancy recovered sooner after giving birth. Functional profiling revealed a depletion of pathways involved in purine salvage and glutamate degradation during the 3rd trimester. Overall, our study demonstrates that the gut microbiome undergoes substantial changes during pregnancy, and the stability of these microbial communities predicts postpartum maternal health and potentially influence lifetime reproductive output.

papers.title: Relatedness and last male sperm precedence in Cheilomenes sexmaculata: Implications for inbreeding avoidance
papers.abstract: Avoidance to mate with relatives is a common evolutionary strategy, as it helps maintain genetic diversity and overall fitness within populations. Females often prefer unrelated males to mitigate the risks associated with inbreeding, such as the expression of deleterious recessive alleles. This preference can involve various post-copulatory mechanisms through which females bias paternity towards males with potentially better genes. The phenomenon of last male sperm precedence, where the last male to mate with a female tends to sire the majority of offspring, is well-documented in ladybird beetles. However, how relatedness affects this phenomenon remains unclear. This study aims to investigate whether paternity share is altered when the last male to mate with a female is related to her. By conducting double mating experiments with two different morphs (typical and intermediate) as phenotypic markers, we seek to determine if relatedness disrupts last male sperm precedence. It was hypothesised that females of Cheilomenes sexmaculata will prefer unrelated males over related ones, irrespective of mating order, potentially breaking down the last male sperm precedence. This preference for unrelated males was reflected in our results with unrelated males exhibiting enhanced reproductive success. Females were more fecund and exhibited higher egg viability with unrelated males. Greater paternity share was observed for unrelated males when the second male was related to the female. This study highlights the dynamic nature of sperm precedence and the role of mate quality in female mate choice, emphasizing the importance of inbreeding avoidance in sexual selection.

papers.title: Dipteran wing damage discriminates between flight motor inertial-elastic distributions
papers.abstract: Insects frequently experience irreversible wing damage, yet many maintain flight by adjusting their wingbeat. In Diptera, wingbeat frequency generally increases as wing inertia is lost, but considerably less than predicted by classical models of the flight motor. In this work, we use an inverse-problem approach to identify passive mechanical features of the dipteran flight motor that explain this discrepancy and reproduce experimentally-observed frequency scaling. Combining spatially resolved reconstruction of wing inertia and motor elasticity, finite-element analysis of thoracic deformation, and data-driven viscoelastic models of asynchronous flight muscle, we identify that a compounding interaction between wing root flexion, wing aerodynamics, and muscular viscoelasticity explain the depressed scaling of wingbeat frequency with loss of inertia. Wing inertia is strongly non-uniform and dominated by the vein structure, leading to further depression with respect to loss of area. But, by contrast, thoracic effective inertia is negligible across a wide array of Dipterans and does not contribute to damage-related scaling. Together these results indicate that much of the dipteran flight motor's responses to wing damage can emerge passively from interactions between the wing, thorax, and muscles; and suggest that a hybrid-elastic architecture with a compliant wing root may be widespread across Diptera. More broadly, we identify wing damage as a tool that can quantitatively discriminate between different candidate models of the insect flight motor, and suggest that altered motor operating conditions can identify mechanical properties difficult to infer from intact flight alone.

papers.title: Long-term storage of Hermetia illucens (Diptera: Stratiomyidae) larvae
papers.abstract: The production of black soldier fly larvae (BSFL), Hermetia illucens (L. 1758) (Diptera: Stratiomyidae), for organic waste conversion and sustainable biomass production is gaining increasing interest. Maintaining sufficient larval stocks is essential for continuous production, yet practical methods for long-term storage remain limited. This study evaluated the effects of temperature (15{degrees}C and 27{degrees}C), larval density, and substrate coverage on BSFL survival and growth over a 12-week storage period. Storage conditions significantly affected substrate moisture, larval survival, and development. Covering the substrate with hydrated straw pellets and aluminium foil reduced water loss and minimised maintenance requirements. The highest survival rate, approximately 70% after two months of storage, was obtained at 15{degrees}C using this combination of hydrated straw pellets and aluminium foil. Following storage, larvae showed high survival and pupal hatching rates under standard rearing conditions, indicating that prolonged storage did not compromise larval fitness. These results demonstrate that storage at 15{degrees}C with hydrated straw pellets and an aluminium cover provides a practical, low-maintenance strategy for maintaining reserve BSFL stocks and ensuring a stable supply of larvae for production and research purposes.

papers.title: Larval thermal tolerances and future dispersal potential of the subtropical-to-temperate sea urchin Tripneustes australiae
papers.abstract: The distribution and dispersal of marine ectotherms is mediated by their thermal tolerances, and as the oceans warm species distributions are shifting. Developmental thermal tolerances of marine invertebrates with a pelagic life-history phase can be used to predict the potential for local extinctions and range extensions. In southeast Australia, Tripneustes australiae is an ecologically important sea urchin species as it undergoes periodic outbreaks and can transform ecosystems through intense herbivory. We investigated the embryonic and early larval developmental tolerances of T. australiae with respect to its current distribution, to predict current and future dispersal capacity. The optimal thermal window for survival, normal development and developmental progression of T. australiae ranged between 17 and 23{degrees}C, with probability of survival at these temperatures remaining above 85% throughout the experiment. This developmental thermal window overlaps with the current thermal regime experienced across the adult distribution. This suggests that T. australiae may have a similar thermal window in its adult and early larval life history stages. Further, T. australiae may have the potential to persist at its warm-range edge into the future and to disperse and range shift poleward in coming decades. Indeed, we show that the temperature at which larvae have a 50% probability of survival may extend poleward across the Bass Strait by 2100. The persistence of T. australiae in its mid-range, its potential to disperse poleward, and increased grazing pressure from periodic outbreaks, may impact temperate macroalgal habitats already at risk from warming and concentrated grazing by other sea urchin taxa.

papers.title: Distribution of midleg campaniform sensilla in Hemiptera and their association with vibrational communication
papers.abstract: Campaniform sensilla are cuticular strain receptors that contribute to locomotion, postural control and vibration detection in insects. Their distribution in Hemiptera remains incompletely documented, limiting comparative and experimental investigation of their possible role in vibrational communication. We used scanning electron microscopy to map externally recognisable campaniform sensilla on the midlegs of a phylogenetically broad sample of Hemiptera, with an emphasis on Heteroptera. We recorded sensilla number and location by leg segment, distinguished between confidently identified sensilla and candidate structures, and compared counts between taxa with documented vibrational communication and those without a published record. We found widespread high concentration of campaniform sensilla across Heteroptera, although the distribution of sensilla on other leg segments was more variable. The sampled Pentatomoidea Trichophora had particularly high counts, and the exploratory comparison indicated higher counts in taxa with documented vibroacoustic communication. This association requires cautious interpretation because communication is incompletely documented, sampling is limited, and sensilla number may also reflect shared ancestry, leg mechanics and other sensory functions. Our survey provides a comparative anatomical basis for testing how campaniform sensilla contribute to vibration perception in Hemiptera.

papers.title: Rapid interannual reorganisation of Whiskered Tern Chlidonias hybrida breeding colonies within an urban wetland network
papers.abstract: Colonial waterbirds breeding in unstable wetland habitats are expected to show flexible colony-site use, but how breeding activity redistributes within small networks of alternative nesting sites, particularly in urban wetlands, is poorly documented. We quantified the spatial organisation of breeding Whiskered Terns Chlidonias hybrida across nine lakes of Vacaresti Natural Park, a spontaneously developed urban wetland in Bucharest, Romania, using nest counts repeated every one to three weeks over four breeding seasons (2022-2025). The number of occupied lakes fell from nine in 2022 to three in 2024, before a partial recovery to six in 2025, while the annual peak of simultaneously active nests ranged from 53 (2024) to 222 (2025). Spatial concentration at the annual peak survey was higher in 2024-2025 (dominant-lake proportion 0.55-0.56; Simpson's concentration index C = 0.42-0.50) than in 2022-2023 (0.41-0.46; C = 0.29-0.32), and the peak-survey distributions of 2024 and 2025 showed no overlap (Bray-Curtis dissimilarity = 1.0). The breeding season was long and asynchronous in 2022, when the largest colony shifted repeatedly among lakes, but compressed and synchronised in 2024-2025, when a single lake remained dominant throughout the season. Lake surface area (0.18-2.25 ha) was not detectably associated with occupancy or seasonal maximum nest numbers. These results indicate highly flexible colony-site use and rapid interannual reorganisation of breeding activity within a compact network of alternative nesting sites. Conservation and monitoring of urban wetland colonies should therefore encompass the entire network of potential nesting sites rather than only the currently dominant colony site.

papers.title: Interspecific faecal microbiota transplantation tests microbial contributions to thermal physiology in lizards
papers.abstract: While the influence of microorganisms in the thermal physiology of animals is increasingly recognised, the role of the gut microbiome in enhancing phenotypic plasticity remains underexplored, particularly in ectotherms. Here, we tested the effect of gut microbiomes in modulating the physiological response of lizards to sudden temperature fluctuations. In captivity, we conducted an experiment with wild-caught Podarcis lizards: Mediterranean Podarcis liolepis (n=9) adapted to warm and dry environments, and Atlantic P. muralis (n=18) adapted to cooler and wetter conditions. Animals were assigned to three groups (intervention, control-cold and control-warm) and subjected to microbiota manipulations using antibiotics and faecal microbiota transplants (FMT). In the intervention group, cold-adapted P. muralis received faecal suspension from warm-adapted P. liolepis, while control-cold and control-warm groups received intraspecific transplants. Microbiome variation was analysed through genome-resolved metagenomics of 162 faecal samples, yielding 313 MAGs across 15 phyla, containing almost 1M annotated genes. One week after transplantation, microbiomes of control animals differed from their original state, whereas those of the intervention group (P. muralis), transitioned to a state resembling P. liolepis. After two weeks, both control groups showed trends of reversing their microbiomes to their original states. However, the intervention group displayed a distinct trajectory, resembling the microbial donors'. Although potentially relevant trends were observed, these microbiome alterations did not translate into detectable significant differences in their thermal physiology. Nevertheless, our results provide proof of concept for microbial transplants in lizards, and opportunities to further explore the link between gut microbes and host physiological responses in ectotherms.

papers.title: Green turtle satellite telemetry: identifying spatial movements, residency patterns, and habitat associations in Aotearoa New Zealand
papers.abstract: Sea turtle conservation relies largely on the identification of ecologically significant marine areas. Green sea turtles (Chelonia mydas) are resident in Aotearoa New Zealand waters, yet much of their spatial ecology remains undefined. To address this, satellite telemetry was used to map juvenile and sub-adult green sea turtle spatial movements, residency patterns, and habitat associations. Our findings provide the first evidence of individual fine-scale habitat use and long-term residency in New Zealand waters. Data will contribute to regional and global efforts to identify ecologically significant sea turtle habitat, including Important Marine Turtle Areas (IMTAs) and Blue Corridors for Turtles (BC4T), and help advance conservation efforts.

papers.title: Corazonin links social role and metabolic-stress responses in honey bee workers
papers.abstract: Corazonin is implicated in regulating diverse behavioral and physiological responses in insects, yet its role in honey bees remains unclear. Work in social and non-social species suggests an ancestral function for corazonin as a metabolic stress signal and a derived function as a pro-foraging signal in social insects. To investigate this hypothesis, we examined corazonin signaling across worker roles and metabolic states and tested its regulatory relationships with pathways central to worker division of labor. Central corazonin levels (both transcript and peptide) were approximately threefold higher in foragers than in nurses. Acute metabolic challenge did not alter brain corazonin but strongly upregulated fat body corazonin receptor (CrzR) transcript in nurses only, suggesting role-specific induction of peripheral sensitivity to corazonin signaling. Injection of synthetic corazonin decreased fat body insulin receptor substrate transcript, while transcripts of vitellogenin (Vg), unpaired-like A, ecdysone receptor B, and Cyp314a1 were unaffected. Measures of gustatory responsiveness, starvation resistance, and hemolymph sugar levels were similarly unaffected by corazonin injection. Reducing Vg through RNA interference in nurse-age bees did not affect CrzR transcript levels, despite vitellogenin's established roles in stress buffering, antioxidant defense, and lifespan. This contrast highlights the specificity of CrzR upregulation in nurses as a response to metabolic challenge rather than general stress. Together, these findings support corazonin as a co-opted nutritional signal that helps shape the forager physiological state, suggesting that it may act in part through interactions with insulin signaling rather than directly regulating classical nutritional or stress-response pathways.

papers.title: Pseudocryptic diversity within the Phakellia robusta species complex: description of Phakellia pallida sp. nov. and Phakellia pusilla sp. nov.
papers.abstract: The genus Phakellia comprises predominantly fan-shaped deep-sea sponges, but its species diversity and boundaries remain unresolved. Here, we use an integrative approach combining morphological and molecular data to investigate the Phakellia robusta species complex and describe two new species, Phakellia pallida sp. nov. and Phakellia pusilla sp. nov. Overlap in external and spicular morphology makes these taxa challenging to identify. Molecular analyses based on mitochondrial (cox1) and nuclear (28S) markers support the recognition of the three taxa as distinct species, and reveal their close evolutionary relationship. The two new species co-occur in the NE Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea, with overlapping depth ranges, although P. pallida sp. nov. is generally found at greater depths. Our results also suggest that several previous records of P. robusta from the Mediterranean and southern parts of the NE Atlantic may instead correspond to either P. pallida sp. nov. or P. pusilla sp. nov., indicating that its distribution requires reassessment. In addition, a group I intron previously reported in the cox1 gene of P. robusta was polymorphically detected at the same insertion site in some, but not all, individuals of P. pusilla sp. nov., but it was absent from P. pallida sp. nov. individuals. Overall, our results reveal pseudocryptic diversity within Phakellia and highlight the value of integrative approaches for resolving species boundaries and reassessing deep-sea sponge diversity and distributions.

papers.title: First confirmed record in Melilla of Gerbillus campestris Loche, 1867 (Muridae: Gerbillinae) for Spain
papers.abstract: The fieldwork was carried out between December 2023 and June 2025, with the aim, among others, of confirming the possible presence of the North African Gerbil (Gerbillus campestris) in Melilla. To this end, 56 camera trap stations were installed, each equipped with a camera trap. Of the total number of camera trap stations installed, the presence of Gerbillus campestris was detected in six of them, representing a capture success rate of 10.71%. Following the detection of the species, a specimen was captured using cage traps. For identification purposes, samples of epithelial tissue from the ear and faeces were collected. These samples were sent to the Institute of Vertebrate Biology of the Czech Academy of Sciences, Brno, Czech Republic, for analysis. There, DNA was extracted from the samples using the Innu PREP DNA Mini Kit 2.0 (IST Innuscreen GmbH, Germany) according to the manufacturer's protocol. The results obtained confirm, for the first time through records of the species, the presence of Gerbillus campestris in Melilla and, therefore, in Spain and Europe.

papers.title: Ground-nesting bee survival after soil translocation and disturbance
papers.abstract: Ground-nesting wild bees require suitable soil conditions for their below-ground development and overwintering life stages. Understanding how soil translocation and disturbance affect individuals and the following generations of bees is important for identifying conservation measures for ground-nesting wild bees. We investigated the effects of soil translocation and disturbance on the ground-nesting solitary spring mining bee Colletes cunicularius. In a replicated controlled design, we compared the effects of soil translocation with different degrees of disturbance on the number of surviving bees and the emergence time. We found that soil translocation and disturbance reduced bee survival but did not result in complete mortality, with some individuals surviving even under severe soil disturbance. There was no evidence that soil disturbance affected the timing of spring emergence, suggesting that disturbance is unlikely to alter the timing of nest construction and, consequently, the production of the next generation. Our results indicate that translocating soil containing overwintering bees could be a promising conservation measure to compensate for habitat loss caused by land conversion.

papers.title: Artificial light at night and concealment level affect detection probability of stranded seabirds: a study with 3D-printed puffin decoys
papers.abstract: Fledglings of burrow-nesting seabirds are vulnerable to disorientation by artificial light at night (ALAN) and grounding in coastal human settlements, where most individuals presumably perish if not rescued. Accurate estimates of the effects of stranding on seabird populations remain elusive due to several levels of uncertainty, such as the number of stranded seabirds estimated to remain undiscovered by rescuers. One species subjected to stranding is the Atlantic puffin (Fratercula arctica). We hypothesized that the detection probability of puffin fledglings by the Puffin Patrol rescue program, operating in Newfoundland, Canada, is affected by light level, concealment level, and search effort. We deployed realistic puffin decoys in locations of varying light and concealment levels throughout two sites that are searched nightly by rescuers and measured the amount of time and search effort required until each decoy was found. Approximately 78% more search effort was required to find a decoy in darkness (32.0 min) compared with illuminated conditions (18.0 min), and up to 100% more search effort was required to find a decoy placed in concealed conditions (35.5 min) than one in the open (17.5 min). After two hours of searching, on average over 10% of decoys were still not found, although each additional minute of search effort increased detection rate of an individual decoy by 0.6%. In combination with recent advances in our knowledge of seabird post-stranding behaviour, our study offers a first step in the development of correction factors which can be adapted to site- and species-specific requirements of other rescue programs around the world that rely on volunteers to search for stranded birds. Application of such correction factors will hopefully result in better estimation of mortality rates and their resultant effects on populations.

papers.title: Bill colour outperforms iris colour for sexing in Starlings Sturnus vulgaris in breeding condition
papers.abstract: Reliable morphological criteria for sexing birds without the need for invasive procedures are scientifically and ethically valuable. Smith et al (2005) reported that iris colour assigns the genetic sex of Starlings Sturnus vulgaris with 98% accuracy, and bill base colour with 100% accuracy when birds are in breeding condition, but these figures have not been tested independently. We applied their criteria to 31 captive Starlings in breeding condition, using three observers blind to genetic sex, two of them new to Starling sexing. Bill base colour correctly predicted genetic sex for all 29 birds scored, with complete observer agreement. Mean iris score was correct for 27 of 31 (87.1%), fewer than the 94 of 96 reported by Smith et al (2005) for birds in breeding condition (Fisher exact test, P = 0.031), although with so few errors in either study this comparison is imprecise. Observer agreement was high, so these errors reflect iris colouration conflicting with genetic sex rather than inconsistent scoring; bill base colour was correct for all four misassigned birds. Body mass and tarsus length classified 77% and 58% of birds correctly, their published thresholds missing in opposite directions. We conclude that bill base colour should be the primary criterion for sexing Starlings in breeding condition; the accuracy of iris colour should not be assumed to be 98%.

papers.title: Comparing the Influence of Habitat Configuration on Population Connectivity and Genetic Structure Using Congeneric Species Across Multiple Taxa
papers.abstract: Abstract Habitat configuration influences population connectivity and, consequently, genetic structure. River networks provide heterogeneous, hierarchically arranged environments that shift drastically from upstream to downstream. We compared congeneric species across Ephemeroptera, Plecoptera, and Trichoptera, emphasizing longitudinal replacement (upstream to downstream) and the rarely studied wet rock (hygropetric) habitats. We surveyed six rivers on the Muroto Peninsula, Japan, qualitatively sampling aquatic insects at 63 sites. Cluster analysis based on the environmental data classified surveyed sites into four clusters. We analyzed a total of 10 species from four genera that exhibit longitudinal replacement patterns within genera. Genetic analyses based on the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase subunit I region revealed that upstream species showed higher genetic diversity than downstream species. In contrast, species adapted to hygropetric exhibited the lowest genetic differentiation among all habitat types. A novel contribution of this study is the inclusion of hygropetric species. The surprisingly low differentiation in hygropetric species suggests high connectivity, similar to lentic species. By comparing congeneric taxa across orders within environmentally similar rivers, we reduce phylogenetic and environmental confounds, strengthening inference that habitat configuration and dispersal traits jointly shape genetic structure. These findings provide a new perspective on riverine spatial ecology and underscore the importance of microhabitat-aware comparisons for evolutionary inference.

papers.title: Late lactation represents the main window for sow-to-piglet transmission of persistent gut strains
papers.abstract: The gut microbiota plays a key role in piglet health, and maternal microbial transmission may represent a promising lever to shape early-life microbiota and prevent post-weaning digestive disorders. This study aimed to better characterize sow-to-piglet microbiota transmission and persistence using a long-read metabarcoding approach targeting the 16S-ITS-23S region. Fecal samples (n = 204) were collected from 17 families, a family being as sow and three of her piglets, at multiple stages: late gestation (G110), early (L6) and late lactation (L28) for sows; early lactation (L6), late lactation (L28), and 5 days post-weaning for piglets. To approximate strain-level resolution, a putative strain (PS) approach was developed by clustering ASVs (n = 6064) affiliated with the same species based on abundance covariance (r > 0.9), resulting in 4857 PS. Piglet microbiota progressively diversified during lactation and converged toward that of sow. In sows, 27 {+/-} 6% of PS were persistent from late gestation to late lactation. In piglets, only 4.2 {+/-} 2.5% of PS persisted from d6 to 5 days post-weaning. Persistent PS in piglets were mainly affiliated with Limosilactobacillus reuteri and Lactobacillus amylovorus followed with Holdemanella porci and H. biformis, Lentihominibacter hominis and Dorea formicigenerans. Shared PS were significantly higher within families than between unrelated pairs (p < 0.05). Maternal transmission peaked at the end of lactation (35 {+/-} 7% at L28). Persistent transmitted PS represented 2.7 {+/-} 1.6% (d6-post-weaning) and 15.4 {+/-} 5.6% (d28-post-weaning). Early-transmitted persistent PS were mainly affiliated with Limosilactobacillus reuteri, Lactobacillus amylovorus, and Paraeggerthella hominis, whereas late-transmitted persistent PS were associated with Prevotella spp., Sphaerochaeta globosa, and Bariatricus comes. These findings highlight the significance of maternal transmission in shaping the post-weaning microbiota and identify late lactation as a critical window for microbiota transfer.

papers.title: RISC-Bound Small RNA Sequencing Provides Insights into Guide Strand Selection and siRNA Trimming and Tailing Following Insecticidal dsRNA Delivery
papers.abstract: RNA interference (RNAi) offers a sequence-specific approach to pest control. In insects, Dicer-2 processes double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) into small interfering RNA (siRNA) duplexes, from which the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) retains a guide strand. Only antisense-loaded RISC can mediate cleavage of the target transcript. However, how sequence features shape the RISC-bound siRNA pool in pests remains poorly understood, limiting opportunities for sequence optimization. Here, we profiled RISC-bound siRNAs following injection of 34 insecticidal dsRNAs targeting 11 essential genes in Tribolium castaneum larvae. We computationally reconstructed 7,879 siRNA pairs and examined associations between sequence features and strand bias. Differences in GC identity at terminal paired positions 1 to 5, used as a proxy for local thermodynamic asymmetry, correlated with strand bias, with the strongest correlations at the first two paired positions. ORF targeting and reduced predicted antisense self-folding were also associated with higher antisense fractions. Analysis of non-templated terminal additions revealed predominantly 3-prime uridylation, a known signature of small RNA turnover, along with putative 3-prime trimming. Among ORF-associated siRNA pairs, sense strands showed higher relative U-tailing abundance, based on 3-prime uridylated and putatively trimmed-and-3-prime-uridylated reads relative to perfect 21-nt reads, than antisense strands. Antisense strands with the least predicted self-folding also showed low relative U-tailing abundance. These observations are consistent with sequence-dependent contributions from both guide-strand selection and differential post-RISC-loading siRNA retention, although a causal link remains to be established. The identified associations provide a basis for testing whether dsRNA sequence optimization can improve pest control efficacy and reduce off-target activity.

papers.title: Uterocalin: a protein uniquely specialised to support mobile encapsulated embryos of horses, rhinos and tapirs
papers.abstract: Equids are considered unique in having encapsulated embryos that are actively moved between the uteri of mares during the first two and three weeks of pregnancy and do not form a placenta until about 40 days, the longest pre-placentation period known amongst Eutheria. Their embryos are likely supplied through the glycoprotein capsule with selected nutrients by uterocalin, a carrier protein secreted by maternal endometrial glands. Uterocalin binds polyunsaturated fatty acids and retinol (Vitamin A), concentrates in the capsule, and is internalised by the embryo. Here it is shown that the structures of equid uterocalin comprise an excess of metabolism-related essential amino acids, and structural specialisations potentially involved in stabilising the capsule matrix until emergence and engagement with a receptor on the trophoblast surface. The genomes of other perissodactyls (rhinos and tapirs) encode uterocalins with amino acid sequences, excesses of essential amino acids, and predicted structural properties, all closely similar to horse uterocalin. These characteristics are unique to the perissodactyl uterocalins and are not found in similar proteins of other mammal groups. Hence, rhinos and tapirs probably have equid-like reproductive specialisations retained since before the Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction and that uterocalin is key to both embryo nutrition and capsule formation.

papers.title: Evolutionary and multi-omic divergences associated with the extreme sexual size dimorphism in spiders
papers.abstract: Extreme sexual size dimorphism (SSD) represents one of the most striking forms of phenotypic divergence between the sexes, yet the genomic basis of extreme body-size dimorphism remains poorly understood. Orb-weaving spiders exhibit some of the most pronounced female-biased SSD among terrestrial arthropods, providing an exceptional system for investigating the evolutionary and genomic changes associated with extreme SSD. Here, we combined comparative genomics across 51 spider species with sex-resolved transcriptomic and chromatin profiling in the highly dimorphic Joro spider, Trichonephila clavata. Across spiders, we identified SSD-associated evolutionary-rate shifts in genes involved in chromatin regulation, growth, and cuticle structural organization. We further found a significant positive association between JHAMT copy number and SSD, with larger gene repertoires occurring in more extremely dimorphic lineages. In T. clavata, expanded JHAMT paralogs showed sex- and tissue-biased expression together with sex-specific differences in chromatin accessibility and local chromatin interactions. Integrated multi-omic analyses further revealed coordinated sex-specific differences in transcription, chromatin accessibility, and chromatin interactions across genes involved in ecdysteroid signaling, insulin and growth regulation, and epidermal and cuticular processes. Altogether, these findings provide insight into the evolutionary and regulatory changes associated with extreme female-biased SSD in spiders.

papers.title: Avian Diversity and Community Structure in Magadh University Campus Landscape, Bodh Gaya
papers.abstract: University campuses function as important refugia for biodiversity within an increasingly urbanizing landscape. Magadh University (MU) is among the oldest universities of Bihar, India, located in Bodh Gaya, a place of spiritual tourism, near a UNESCO heritage site. The campus hosts a mosaic of heterogeneous habitats, rich vegetation and dense canopy cover along with varied range of anthropogenic interferences. This study mainly focusses on measuring the alpha diversity of avifaunal species and persistence across four seasons from July 2025 to June 2026, in the peri-urban landscape of MU. A total of 78 bird species belonging to 41 families and 16 orders were recorded using a combination of point count, line transect and acoustic monitoring. The study revealed that the order Passeriformes was the most species-rich (47.44%). Muscicapidae was the most species-rich family (6 species). Relatively high Shannon diversity (H') = 3.278, low Simpson's dominance (D = 0.062) and a high Pielou's evenness (J) = 0.751 indicated the avian community was distributed across diverse assemblage. Species richness estimates from Chao1 (78.5), iChao1 (79.02) and ACE (79.53) were comparable to recorded 78 species, indicating sampling completeness. Observed species were further classified into five major feeding guilds, majority of which were insectivorous species. 77 of the observed species were classified as Least Concern while Coracias benghalensis was categorized as Near Threatened. These findings demonstrate that the MU campus supports significant taxonomic, functional and temporal avian assemblage, highlighting the conservation values of the campus landscapes within rapidly urbanizing regions.

papers.title: The second life of collection - how the scientific value of natural history holdings can be deliberately increased
papers.abstract: Natural history collections cannot be assessed by the size of their holdings, because their scientific value is a multidimensional and dynamic property that can be deliberately shaped. The authors argue that this value can be systematically increased through purposeful curatorial and research actions, both without acquiring new material and through its continuous replenishment. We propose an analytical framework for describing the scientific value of a collection, based on five dimensions: epistemic distinctiveness, data integrity and accessibility, documented and potential research applications, unique taxonomic status, and compliance with ethical and legal standards. The framework is complemented by a dynamic perspective describing the conditions under which the value of a collection rises and falls over time. We then present a typology of actions that increase collection value incrementally, distinguishing four categories according to the object of the action: (i) enriching the data record, (ii) enriching the physical specimen, (iii) establishing formal status, and (iv) increasing visibility and interoperability. Each category of actions is linked to the corresponding dimensions of scientific value, so that the typology and the framework together form a single analytical tool. Both perspectives are illustrated with two collections deposited in the Natural History Collections of Adam Mickiewicz University in Pozna[n]. The first is an acarological collection of soil samples together with its derivatives, comprising collections of nomenclatural types, microscope slides, SEM images and molecular sequences deposited in global gene banks. The second is a conchological and virtual collection of the Roman snail (Helix pomatia), which illustrates the transition from a set of physical specimens to a resource of spatial digital data. The proposed approach provides practical tools for planning collection development, for communicating the importance of collections to funding bodies, and for identifying the untapped research potential of existing holdings.

papers.title: Aerodynamic performance appears to have shaped the evolution of flight-feather microstructures
papers.abstract: Flight feather structures - shaft, barbs, and barbules - have transformed through evolution. Although size, shape and orientation of these structures likely influence the aerodynamic performance of the feathers, their impact remains unclear. Here we investigated the feather structures influence on flow and aerodynamic performance, using computational fluid dynamic modelling, by modifying the morphology of a section of a Jackdaw (Corvus monedula) flight feather. We show that the flow over the leading vane is a key factor, and that changing the barb-to-shaft angle from its natural state as well as the trailing vane barb angle, reduces performance, which could explain evolutionary changes from early Paraves species. All in all, our results suggest that current feather composition may be close to a local maximum for both aerodynamic efficiency and stability/flow predictability, suggesting evolution of feather structures have been driven by aerodynamic performance, which should have implications for designing bio-inspired technologies.
